turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

That sounds incredibly heavy. “Handle” can feel like code for *make the problem disappear*, especially when the person has decades of trust and status behind him. But you don’t have to choose between protecting the releases and humiliating or scapegoating Suresh-ji.

The conversation should be about the module, the missed commitments, and what needs to change—not his age, tenure, or reputation. Go in with specific facts and genuine respect:

> “Suresh-ji, I want to talk openly about the last two releases. The module slipped on X and Y, which affected the overall dates. I respect your experience, and I also need to be clear that this can’t continue. I want to understand what’s causing the risk—technical complexity, capacity, dependencies, or something else—and agree on a concrete recovery plan.”

Then listen carefully, but don’t let empathy turn into vagueness. Agree on milestones, ownership, support, and a near-term checkpoint. If the issue is beyond his capacity or the module needs redesign/staffing changes, say that plainly and involve your director with documentation.

You’re not being disloyal by managing performance. In fact, giving him a clear chance to respond and recover is more respectful than quietly building a case around him. And before the meeting, clarify with your director what “handle” actually means: a recovery plan, role change, reassignment, or formal performance action. Don’t let an ominous word force you into guessing.

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

Oh, that’s not just a performance conversation—it feels like a betrayal of someone who once protected and cared for you. No wonder the metrics feel almost cruel in your hands.

But you don’t have to erase that history to be his manager now. You can honor it directly, without turning the conversation into an apology or avoiding the issue:

> “Suresh-ji, this is difficult for me because you’ve supported me since I was new here. I haven’t forgotten the night you stayed late to help me, or how you’ve looked out for me. I also need to speak with you honestly in my role as your manager. The last two releases slipped, and the current quality and predictability aren’t sustainable.”

Then don’t lead with a slide deck. Lead with a private, human conversation. Bring the defect data as evidence, not as a prosecution exhibit—perhaps one concise summary rather than a wall of metrics. Ask him what he sees:

> “Do you believe these numbers reflect the real problem? What am I missing?”

You can be grateful and accountable at the same time. His past kindness doesn’t mean he gets immunity from feedback; your present responsibility doesn’t mean you have to treat him like a disposable underperformer.

And be careful not to say “you’re like family” or “I owe you” in a way that makes the expectations ambiguous. The kindest version is clear: *I respect you, I’m grateful to you, and this needs to improve.*

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

Yes—the basic plan is right: private, direct, specific, and respectful. You’re not wrong to address it, and withholding the feedback would only make the situation harder.

One important adjustment: don’t make Monday a one-way metrics presentation. Use the data to establish the impact, then ask for his perspective and agree on a concrete recovery plan.

You can say:

> “I want to discuss the last two releases and the risks in your module. We had defects X and Y, and they contributed to slips of Z. This needs to improve. I’d like to understand what’s driving it, and then agree on milestones, support, and a checkpoint.”

That is candid without being punitive. You don’t need to become cold to be professional, and you don’t need to pretend your history with him doesn’t matter. Go in steady, not spiralling. The goal is clarity and improvement—not delivering a verdict.

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

You may not be able to find a version where nobody feels hurt. That’s different from being the villain.

If, after clear feedback and real support, the role still isn’t working, a PIP or reassignment may be the responsible outcome. It wouldn’t erase what he did for you, and it wouldn’t mean you used his trust against him. It would mean you took seriously both his dignity and the team’s obligations—by being honest rather than quietly letting the module, and possibly his reputation, deteriorate.

And “let him coast” isn’t necessarily kindness. It could leave him attached to work he can no longer safely carry, expose the team to more failures, and postpone a conversation he deserves to have while there’s still time to respond.

You also don’t have to carry this decision alone. Tell your director plainly:

> “I’m committed to giving him a fair opportunity with defined expectations and support. If he doesn’t meet them, I want the next steps to follow a consistent process—not be an informal push-out. I also want to explore whether there’s a role or scope where his experience is a better fit.”

Document expectations and support, involve HR or your people partner as required, and ask whether comparable cases are handled the same way. That protects him, you, and the company.

You can say to Suresh-ji, if it comes to that:

> “I’m grateful for everything you’ve done for me. This decision isn’t a judgment on your worth or the years you’ve given here. It’s about the requirements of this role and what we’ve been able to establish together.”

It may still hurt. But causing disappointment through honest, fair management is not the same as betraying someone.
